text: Nokia Corporation, a Finnish multinational telecommunications, information technology, and consumer electronics corporation, was originally established in 1865 as a pulp mill by mining engineer Fredrik Idestam near Tampere, Finland, with a second mill opened in Nokia in 1868. The company was formally named Nokia Ab in 1871 after the second site. Over time, it expanded into rubber and cables, and in 1922 partnered with Finnish Rubber Works and Kaapelitehdas. In 1967, the three entities merged to form Nokia Corporation, which was restructured into forestry, cable, rubber, and electronics, later entering networking and radio industries. In 1977, Kari Kairamo became CEO and led major acquisitions, including Salora, Luxor AB, and Oceanic, making Nokia the third-largest television manufacturer in Europe. In 1979, Nokia established Mobira, a mobile radio telephone manufacturer, which launched the world's first international cellular network, NMT, in 1981 and the first mobile phone, the Mobira Senator, in 1982. In 1984, Nokia acquired Mobira and later acquired Schaub-Lorenz in 1987, which was sold under the "ITT Nokia" brand. In 1988, Nokia bought Ericsson's Information Systems division, forming Nokia Data. After Kairamo's death in 1988, Simo Vuorilehto led a restructuring, divesting unstrategic units, including Nokian Tyres in 1988 and Finnish Rubber Works in 1990, and selling the computer division, Nokia Data, to ICL in 1991. Jorma Ollila succeeded Vuorilehto in 1992 and transformed the company into a telecom-oriented enterprise, leading to a significant rise in operating profit from negative in 1991 to $1 billion in 1995 and nearly $4 billion by 1999. Nokia assisted in developing the GSM standard and launched the world's first GSM call in 1991 using its equipment. The Nokia 1011 was the first commercially available GSM mobile phone, launched in November 1992. In 1996, Nokia sold its television business to Semi-Tech Corporation, closing its German plant in September 1996 and retaining brand rights until 1999. In 1997, Nokia launched the first digital satellite receivers in the UK and introduced the first with Common Interface (CI) support. In 1998, Nokia became the world's best-selling mobile phone brand, surpassing Motorola, and manufactured its 100 millionth mobile phone. The success was driven by fashion-oriented products like the Nokia 5110 and 3210, featuring colorful, replaceable back covers. In 1998, Nokia co-founded Symbian Ltd. with Psion to develop a new operating system for PDAs and smartphones, launching the Nokia 9210 Communicator in 2001 and the Symbian Series 60 platform, later introducing the Nokia 7650 as the first camera phone. Nokia became the largest shareholder of Symbian in February 2004 and fully acquired the company in June 2008, forming the Symbian Foundation as its successor. In 1999, Nokia introduced its first wireless LAN products and in 2000 employed over 55,000 people, with a 30% market share in mobile phones, nearly double that of Motorola. By 2000, Nokia had operations in 140 countries and was recognized as the "most trusted brand in Europe" in a Reader's Digest survey. Nokia pioneered camera phones, launching the first in North America with the Nokia 3600/3650 in 2003, and introduced the Nseries in April 2005. The Nokia N95, launched in 2006, won "best mobile imaging device" in Europe in 2007, while the N82 (2008) and N93 (2006) were also recognized for imaging. The N8 (2010) featured a 12-megapixel sensor, the 808 PureView (2012) had a 41-megapixel sensor, and the Lumia 920 (2012) implemented advanced PureView technologies. Nokia was a pioneer in mobile gaming, with Snake preloaded on many devices, and attempted to enter the handheld gaming market with the N-Gage in 2002, which failed despite efforts to revive it as a smartphone platform in 2008. In Q1 2004, Nokia's mobile phone market share dropped to 28.9%, but it recovered, reaching a peak of 40.4% in Q4 2007 with a 51% smartphone market share, being the largest vendor globally in all regions except North America. In 2005, Nokia launched mobile TV trials in Finland with Yle and in the UK with Arqiva and O2 using the DVB-H standard. In 2005, Nokia developed Maemo, a Linux-based operating system, which shipped on the Nokia 770 Internet Tablet. On 1 June 2006, Jorma Ollila became chairman and retired as CEO, replaced by Olli-Pekka Kallasvuo. In August 2007, Nokia introduced Ovi, an umbrella for its Internet services, including the N-Gage platform and Nokia Music Store, which faced competition from Apple's App Store in 2008. In October 2008, Nokia announced the Nokia 5800 Xpress. In 2020, Nokia employed approximately 92,000 people across over 100 countries, did business in more than 130 countries, and reported annual revenues of around €23 billion. It is a public limited company listed on Nasdaq Helsinki and the New York Stock Exchange, was the world's 415th-largest company by 2016 revenues according to the Fortune Global 500, having peaked at 85th place in 2009, and is a component of the Euro Stoxx 50 stock market index. The company's roots are in the Tampere region of Pirkanmaa, with its main headquarters in Espoo, Finland, in the Helsinki metropolitan area. At its peak in 2000, Nokia accounted for 4% of Finland's GDP, 21% of total exports, and 70% of the Nasdaq Helsinki market capital. Nokia is the world's third-largest network equipment manufacturer as of 2018. After a partnership with Microsoft and subsequent market struggles, Microsoft bought Nokia's mobile phone business in 2014, incorporating it as Microsoft Mobile. Following the sale, Nokia focused on telecommunications infrastructure and Internet of things technologies, divesting its Here mapping division and acquiring Alcatel-Lucent, including its Bell Labs research organization. The company also experimented with virtual reality and digital health through the purchase of Withings. The Nokia brand returned to the mobile and smartphone market in 2016 via a licensing arrangement with HMD. Nokia remains a major patent licensor for most large mobile phone vendors. Its history dates from 1865, with the first pulp mill established near Tampere, and a second near Nokia, and the company was named after the latter site. The coordinates of the original site are 60°13′30″N 24°45′22″E (60.225°N 24.756°E).

Nokia launched mobile TV trials in 2005 in Finland with content from public broadcaster Yle, using the DVB-H standard, and the service could be viewed on the widescreen Nokia 7710 smartphone with a special accessory for receiving DVB-H signals. The company also partnered with Arqiva and O2 to conduct trials in the UK in September 2005. In 2005, Nokia developed a Linux-based operating system called Maemo, which was released that year on the Nokia 770 Internet Tablet. On 1 June 2006, Jorma Ollila became chairman and retired as CEO, replaced by Olli-Pekka Kallasvuo. In August 2007, Nokia introduced Ovi, an umbrella name for its new Internet services, including the N-Gage platform and the Nokia Music Store; the Ovi Store faced strong competition from Apple's App Store when it launched in 2008. In October 2008, Nokia announced the Nokia 5800 XpressMusic, the first device to ship with the touch-centric S60 5th Edition, also known as Symbian^1, the first iteration of the platform since the Symbian Foundation's creation. In November 2008, Nokia announced it would end mobile phone sales in Japan due to low market share. Nokia's global mobile phone market share peaked in 2008 at 38.6 percent. That same year, Nokia acquired Trolltech and its Qt software development, which became a central part of its strategy until 2011 and was eventually sold in 2012. Nokia briefly returned to the computer market with the Booklet 3G netbook in August 2009. In late 2009 and 2010, the music-focused Xseries and consumer-focused Cseries were introduced respectively. In April 2010, Nokia introduced the Nokia N8, the first device to run on Symbian^3, though it was delayed for many months, tarnishing the company's image, especially after the failure of the N97 and increased competition from Apple and Google. On 10 September 2010, Olli-Pekka Kallasvuo was fired as CEO, and Stephen Elop from Microsoft was appointed as CEO, becoming the first non-Finnish director in Nokia's history; investors pressured the board to recruit an outsider to shake up management and break from the traditional "Nokia way." Ollila announced he would step down as chairman by 2012. On 11 March 2011, Nokia paid Elop a $6 million signing bonus as "compensation for lost income from his prior employer," in addition to his $1.4 million annual salary. The old Symbian OS became completely open-source in February 2010, but in November 2010, it was announced that the Symbian Foundation was closing and that Nokia would take back control of the Symbian operating system under closed licensing. By then, Nokia was the only remaining company using the platform, along with carrier NTT Docomo in Japan, after Samsung and Sony Ericsson moved to Android. In 2010, for its Linux ambitions, Nokia collaborated with Intel to form the MeeGo project, resulting from the merger of Nokia's Maemo and Intel's Moblin. Nokia's Symbian platform, which had been the leading smartphone platform in Europe and Asia for many years, became outdated and difficult for developers after the rise of iOS and Android. To counter this, Nokia planned to make its MeeGo Linux operating system, under development, the company's flagship on smartphones. Shortly after Elop's CEO tenure began, the Nokia board approved his ability to change the company's mobile phone strategy, including switching operating systems. Veteran Anssi Vanjoki, head of the smartphones division, left the company around this time, with his final appearance at Nokia World 2010 when the Nokia E7-00 and other Symbian^3 devices were introduced. On 11 February 2011, Nokia announced a "strategic partnership" with Microsoft, adopting Windows Phone 7 as its primary smartphone operating system and integrating its services, including Bing as search engine and Nokia Maps data into Bing Maps. Elop stated that Nokia chose not to use Android due to an apparent inability to "differentiate" its offerings, with critics noting his past ties to Microsoft may have influenced the decision. Although the MeeGo "Harmattan"-based N9 received a highly positive reception in 2011, Nokia had already decided to end MeeGo development and focus solely on its Microsoft partnership, though the CEO said the N9's "innovations" would live on in future products, eventually appearing on the Asha platform in 2013. After the Microsoft partnership announcement, Nokia's market share declined due to falling demand for Symbian as consumers realized the company's focus would shift. The company posted a large loss for the second quarter of 2011—only its second quarterly loss in 19 years. Nokia's first Windows Phone flagship was the Lumia 800, released in November 2011. Falling sales in 2011, not significantly improved by the Lumia line in 2012, led to consecutive quarters of huge losses. By mid-2012, the company's stock price fell below $2. CEO Elop announced cost-cutting measures in June, including shedding 10,000 employees by year-end and closing the Salo manufacturing plant. The Finnish prime minister announced that the government would not subsidize the company from an emergency state fund. Around this time, Nokia launched a new project codenamed "Meltemi," a platform for low-end smartphones. Under the Microsoft alliance and Elop's management, Nokia renewed its focus on the North American market, where Nokia phones had been almost irrelevant for many years. This strategy began in January 2012 with the introduction of the Nokia Lumia 900 smartphone in partnership with U.S. carrier AT&T. In March 2011, Nokia introduced a new corporate typeface called "Pure." On 1 August 2011, Nokia announced a new three-digit naming system for mobile phones, ending the use of letters and effectively ending the Nseries, Eseries, and Cseries; the Nokia 500 was introduced with the new system. Nokia last used three-digit names on analogue phones in the 1990s. When the Lumia 920 was announced in September 2012, it was seen as the first high-end Windows Phone with a feature set capable of challenging rivals, and Elop said the positive reaction created a sense of hope and optimism. The company also made gains in developing countries with its Asha series, which were selling strongly. Although Nokia's smartphone sales and market share increased throughout 2013, including in North America, it was still not enough to avoid financial losses. Ollila stepped down as chairman on 4 May 2012 and was replaced by Risto Siilasmaa. In September 2013, Nokia announced the sale of its mobile and devices division to Microsoft, which helped avoid further financial losses and benefited Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer, who wanted to expand Microsoft's hardware and become a devices and services company. Nokia chairperson Risto Siilasmaa described the deal as rationally correct but emotionally difficult—experts agree that Nokia would have faced a cash crisis without selling the division. Analysts believe Ballmer pushed for the buyout due to fears that Nokia was close to adopting Android and abandoning its Microsoft alliance. Indeed, in January 2014, the Nokia X was introduced, running on a customized version of Android, a surprising launch just weeks before the finalization of the Microsoft buyout. Others, including Ballmer's successor Satya Nadella, believed Microsoft thought merging its software teams with Nokia's hardware engineering and design would "accelerate" growth of Windows Phone. The sale was completed in April 2014, with Microsoft Mobile becoming the successor to Nokia's mobile devices division. Nokia also moved its headquarters to a new building complex at Karaportti. At the time, Ballmer was retiring as Microsoft CEO and was replaced by Satya Nadella, who opposed the Nokia mobile phones purchase, along with chairman Bill Gates. The purchased assets from Nokia were eventually written off by Microsoft in 2015. By 2014, Nokia's global brand value according to Interbrand fell to 98th place, a sharp decline from the 5th place it held in 2009. Nokia's downfall in the mobile phone market has been explained differently by analysts, with many divided over the CEO's decision to abandon its in-house operating system and adopt Windows Phone in 2011. Many researchers concluded that Nokia suffered from deep internal rivalries within management. Former employees claimed that management became complacent after early success. Some from the Symbian development team claimed that upper management rejected hundreds of proposed innovations during the 2000s, including a complete rewrite of Symbian's code. One former employee claimed the company was run as a "Soviet-style bureaucracy." In July 2013, Nokia bought Siemens' stake in the Nokia Siemens Networks joint venture for $2.2 billion, turning it into a wholly owned subsidiary called Nokia Solutions and Networks, later rebranded as Nokia Networks. During its financial struggles, its profitable networking division with Siemens provided much of its income; thus, the purchase was positive, especially after the sale of its mobile devices unit. After selling its mobile devices division, Nokia focused on network equipment through Nokia Networks. In October 2014, Nokia and China Mobile signed a US$970 million framework deal for delivery between 2014 and 2015. On 17 November 2014, Nokia Technologies head Ramzi Haidamus disclosed that the company planned to re-enter the consumer electronics business as an original design manufacturer, licensing in-house hardware designs and technologies to third-party manufacturers. Haidamus stated that the Nokia brand was "valuable" but "is diminishing in value, and that's why it is important that we reverse that trend very quickly, imminently." The next day, Nokia unveiled the N1, an Android tablet manufactured by Foxconn, as its first product following the Microsoft sale. Haidamus emphasized that devices under these licensing agreements would meet high production quality standards and "look and feel just like Nokia built it." Nokia CEO Rajeev Suri stated that the company planned to re-enter the mobile phone business in this manner in 2016, following the expiration of its non-compete clause with Microsoft. According to Robert Morlino, the spokesman for Nokia Technologies, the company planned to follow a brand-licensing model rather than direct marketing of mobile devices due to the sale of its mobile devices division to Microsoft. The company took aggressive steps to revitalize itself, evident through hiring software experts, testing new products, and seeking sales partners. On 14 July 2015, CEO Rajeev Suri confirmed that the company would return to the mobile phones market in 2016. On 28 July 2015, Nokia announced OZO, a 360-degree virtual reality camera with eight 2K optical image sensors, claiming it would be the most advanced VR film-making platform. The division behind the product stated that OZO would be "the first in a planned portfolio of digital media solutions," with more technological products expected. OZO was fully unveiled on 30 November in Los Angeles. The OZO, designed for professional use, was initially intended for retail at US$60,000; however, its price was reduced by $15,000 prior to release and is now listed as $40,000. On 14 April 2015, Nokia confirmed talks with French telecommunications equipment company Alcatel-Lucent regarding a potential merger. The next day, Nokia announced an agreement to purchase Alcatel-Lucent for €15.6 billion in an all-stock deal. CEO Rajeev Suri believed the purchase would give Nokia a strategic advantage in 5G wireless technology development. The acquisition created a stronger competitor to Ericsson and Huawei, whom Nokia and Alcatel-Lucent had surpassed in total combined revenue in 2014. Nokia shareholders hold 66.5% of the new combined company, while Alcatel-Lucent shareholders hold 33.5%. The Bell Labs division was to be maintained, but the Alcatel-Lucent brand would be replaced by Nokia. In October 2015, following approval by China's Ministry of Commerce, the merger awaited approval by French regulators. Despite the initial intent to sell the submarine cable division separately, Alcatel-Lucent later declared it would not. The merger closed on 14 January 2016, but was not complete until 3 November 2016. From the acquisition, Nokia is now also the owner of the Alcatel Mobile phone brand, which continues to be licensed to TCL. On 3 August 2015, Nokia announced a deal to sell its Here digital maps division to a consortium of BMW, Daimler AG, and Volkswagen Group for €2.8 billion. The deal closed on 3 December 2015. On 26 April 2016, Nokia announced its intent to acquire French connected health device maker Withings for US$191 million, integrating it into a new Digital Health unit of Nokia Technologies. Nokia later wrote off the cost of the acquisition and in May 2018 the health unit was sold back to Éric Carreel, a Withings co-founder and former CEO. On 18 May 2016, Microsoft Mobile sold its Nokia-branded feature phone business to HMD Global, a new company founded by former Nokia executive Jean-Francois Baril, and an associated factory in Vietnam to Foxconn's FIH Mobile subsidiary. Nokia entered into a long-term licensing deal with HMD to make it the exclusive manufacturer of Nokia-branded phones and tablets outside Japan, operating in conjunction with Foxconn. The deal also granted HMD the right to essential patents and featurephone software. HMD subsequently announced the Android-based Nokia 6 smartphone in January 2017. At Mobile World Congress, HMD unveiled the Nokia 3 and Nokia 5 smartphones, as well as a re-imagining of Nokia's classic 3310 feature phone. Nokia has direct investments in the company and has some input in the new devices. On 28 June 2016, Nokia demonstrated a 5G-ready network for the first time. In February 2017, Nokia carried out a 5G connection in Oulu, Finland using the 5GTF standard, backed by Verizon, on Intel architecture-based equipment. In July 2017, Nokia and Xiaomi signed a business collaboration agreement and a multi-year patent agreement, including a cross-license to each company's cellular standard-essential patents. In that year, Nokia's brand value was ranked 188th by Brand Finance, a jump of 147 places from 2016, attributed to its health portfolio and new mobile phones developed by HMD Global. In January 2018, Nokia signed a deal with NTT Docomo, Japan's largest mobile operator, to provide 5G wireless radio base stations in the country by 2020. Later that month, Nokia announced the ReefShark line of 5G chipsets, claiming it triples bandwidth to 84 Gbit/s. In 2017, Nokia and Xiaomi signed a business collaboration agreement and a multi-year patent agreement, including a cross-license to each company's cellular standard-essential patents. That year, Nokia's brand value was ranked 188th by Brand Finance, an increase of 147 places from 2016, attributed to its health portfolio and new mobile phones developed by HMD Global. In January 2018, Nokia signed a deal with NTT Docomo, Japan's largest mobile operator, to provide 5G wireless radio base stations in Japan by 2020. Later that month, Nokia announced the ReefShark line of 5G chipsets, claiming it triples bandwidth to 84 Gbit/s. In March 2018, Solidium, the investment arm of the Finnish Government, purchased a 3.3% stake in Nokia valued at €844 million. In May 2018, Nokia acquired a California-based IoT startup, SpaceTime Insight. In January 2019, the Canadian government announced $40 million in support for Nokia's 5G research. A 2019 study by Counterpoint Research found that 96 percent of Nokia phones were either shipped with or updated to the latest Android version since Pie was released in 2018, significantly outperforming competitors like Samsung, LG, Xiaomi, and Huawei, which averaged around 80 percent. On 2 March 2020, Nokia announced Pekka Lundmark as its new CEO. Later that month, Nokia completed the acquisition of Elenion Technologies, a U.S.-based company specializing in silicon photonics technology to improve the economics of advanced optical connectivity products. On 27 May 2020, Sari Baldauf succeeded Risto Siilasmaa as chairwoman of the board of directors, and Kari Stadigh was appointed vice chair. In June 2020, Nokia won a $450 million 5G contract from Taiwan Mobile to build out its next-generation network as the sole supplier. In October 2020, Nokia announced a $14.1 million contract with NASA to build a 4G mobile network for astronaut use on the moon, through its subsidiary Bell Labs, expected to begin in 2022. In 2020, Flipkart collaborated with Nokia to market Nokia-branded consumer products in India, including televisions, a laptop, and a range of air conditioners. In April 2022, Nokia announced it would exit the Russian market following the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, stating the decision would not affect its financial outlook as Russia accounted for less than 2% of Nokia's net sales in 2021. In February 2023, Nokia introduced a new logo for the first time in nearly 60 years to modernize its brand identity, as the previous logo was still associated with mobile phones; the new logo was designed by Lippincott. In December 2023, Nokia acquired Fenix Group to strengthen its wireless offering in the defense segment for an undisclosed amount. In the same month, Nokia announced a €185 million deal with Lumine Group to carve out its device management and service management businesses (inherited from Alcatel-Lucent's purchase of Motive, Inc. and formerly Mformation), with the deal completed in April 2024 and involving the transfer of around 500 employees. In February 2024, Nokia accelerated its carbon neutrality target by 10 years to 2040, having previously committed to cutting its carbon footprint across emissions scopes in half by 2030 from a 2019 baseline. In June 2024, Nokia acquired Infinera for $2.3 billion. On 10 February 2025, Nokia announced that Pekka Lundmark would step down as president and CEO on 31 March and be succeeded by Justin Hotard. In September 2025, Nokia announced an artificial intelligence-based partnership with Supermicro, focusing on integrated data center network products. Nokia is a julkinen osakeyhtiö (public joint-stock company) listed on the Nasdaq Nordic/Helsinki and New York stock exchanges. It plays a major role in Finland's economy, contributing 1.6% to Finland's GDP and accounting for about 16% of the country's exports in 2006, and is a significant employer working with local partners and subcontractors. Nokia comprises two main business groups along with subsidiaries and affiliated firms. Nokia Networks is the largest division, a multinational data networking and telecommunications equipment company headquartered in Espoo, Finland, and the world's third-largest telecoms equipment manufacturer by 2017 revenues (after Huawei and Cisco). It operates in around 150 countries and provides wireless and fixed network infrastructure, communications and network service platforms and professional services to operators and service providers, focusing on GSM, EDGE, 3G/W-CDMA, LTE and WiMAX radio access networks, supporting core networks with increasing IP and multiaccess capabilities and services. The Nokia Siemens Networks (NSN) brand was launched in February 2007 as a 50.1% Nokia and 49.9% Siemens joint venture, now wholly owned by Nokia; in July 2013, Nokia bought back all shares for US$2.21 billion and renamed it first to Nokia Solutions and Networks, then to simply Nokia Networks. Nokia Technologies is a division that develops consumer products and licenses technology including the Nokia brand, focusing on imaging, sensing, wireless connectivity, power management, and materials, and includes three labs: Radio Systems Lab, Media Technologies Lab, and Sensor and Material Technologies Lab; it also runs the Invent with Nokia program. It was created in 2014 following a restructuring. In November 2014, Nokia Technologies launched the Nokia N1 tablet. In July 2015, it introduced the OZO VR camera for professional content creators in Tampere, Finland, featuring 8 synchronized shutter sensors and 8 microphones to capture stereoscopic 3D video and spatial audio; production ended in 2017, but immersive audio software under the OZO brand continues. On 31 August 2016, Ramzi Haidamus stepped down as president of Nokia Technologies, with Brad Rodrigues serving as interim president; on 30 June 2017, Gregory Lee, former CEO of Samsung Electronics in North America, was appointed CEO and president. Nokia Bell Labs, formerly the R&D arm of the American Bell System, became a subsidiary after the 2016 acquisition of Alcatel-Lucent. In December 2023, Nokia announced plans for a new research facility in New Brunswick, New Jersey, relocating from the 80-year-old Bell Labs facility in Murray Hill, New Jersey, expected to occur before 2028. NGP Capital (formerly Nokia Growth Partners) is a global venture capital firm focusing on growth-stage IoT and mobile technology companies, with investments in the U.S., Europe, China, and India; it manages $1 billion in assets after a $350 million funding round in 2016. Nokia had previously promoted innovation through Nokia Venture Partners, renamed BlueRun Ventures and spun off in 2005; the China arm became independent in 2010 as Lanchi Ventures; Nokia Growth Partners was founded in 2005 and renamed to NGP Capital in 2017. NGP's largest exits include GanJi, UCWeb, Whistle, Rocket Fuel, Swype, Summit Microelectronics, and Netmagic. Nuage Networks, formed by Alcatel-Lucent in 2013 to develop software-defined networking solutions, became part of Nokia after the 2016 acquisition; it secured deals with Vodafone and Telefónica in 2017 for its SD-WAN architecture, BT since 2016, and China Mobile in January 2017 for 2,000 public cloud servers, and with China Pacific Insurance Company in October 2017. The company is based in Mountain View, California, with Sunil Khandekar as CEO. Alcatel Mobile, a mobile phone brand owned by Nokia since 2016, was licensed to TCL since 2005 under Alcatel (later Alcatel-Lucent) until 2024. HMD Global, a mobile phone company based in Espoo, Finland, was founded by former Nokia employees and introduced Nokia-branded Android-based devices in 2017; initially, Nokia had no investment but retained some input in device development. Nokia has 10.10% ownership in HMD Global after investing alongside Qualcomm and Google in 2020; in the 2020 financial report, FIH Mobile disclosed a 14.38% ownership, with Finnish Nokia holding 10.10% and other investors including Google, Qualcomm, and others with undisclosed shares. Alcatel Submarine Networks (ASN), a provider of turnkey undersea network solutions, was acquired by Nokia in 2016; it develops technology and offers installation services for optical submarine cable networks globally. Nokia and ASN added the CS Ile d'Ouessant to their fleet in 2019 (originally built as CS Toisa Warrior in 2011) and requested two additional cable ships, CS Ile d'Yeu and CS Ile de Molène, in 2021. The cable-laying fleet includes six from Alcatel, six and seven from Alcatel-Lucent, and eight from Nokia. Key trends for Nokia are as of the financial year ending 31 December. Control and management are divided among shareholders at a general meeting and the Nokia Group Leadership Team, under the direction of the board of directors; the chairman and leadership team members are appointed by the board, with only the chairman belonging to both the board and leadership team. The board has Audit, Personnel, and Corporate Governance and Nomination Committees. Operations are managed under the Finnish Companies Act, Nokia's Articles of Association, and Corporate Governance Guidelines, supplemented by board charters; in November 2019, Nokia discontinued the role of Chief Operating Officer (COO), with Joerg Erlemeier stepping down on 1 January 2020. Nokia is a public limited liability company and the oldest company listed under the same name on the Helsinki Stock Exchange, beginning in 1915; it has had a secondary listing on the New York Stock Exchange since 1994 and shares were delisted from the London, Paris, Stockholm, and Frankfurt stock exchanges in 2003, 2004, 2007, and 2012, respectively; after acquiring Alcatel-Lucent in 2015, it listed again on the Paris Stock Exchange and was included in the CAC 40 index on 6 January 2016 but removed on 18 September 2017. In 2007, Nokia's market capitalization was €110 billion; by 17 July 2012 it fell to €6.28 billion, then rose to €26.0 billion by 23 February 2015; in 2020, it was 21.76 billion. Nokia's corporate culture manifesto since the 1990s is called The Nokia Way, emphasizing speed and flexibility in decision-making within a flat, networked organization. The official business language is English, used in all documentation and official internal communication. In 1992, Nokia adopted values defined by respect, achievement, renewal, and challenge; in May 2007, it redefined them to Engaging You, Achieving Together, Passion for Innovation, and Very Human based on global employee input; in August 2014, after the sale of its Devices business, it reverted to the original 1992 values. Nokia is headquartered at Karaportti in Espoo, Finland, since 2014, after moving from the Nokia House following the sale of the mobile phone business to Microsoft; the Karaportti building was previously the headquarters of NSN (now Nokia Networks). In 2018, Nokia received the Leading Lights award for most innovative cable/video product and was named to Ethisphere's 2018 list of the world's most ethical companies. In 2008, Nokia Siemens Networks reportedly provided Iran's telecom monopoly with technology enabling deep packet inspection to intercept Internet communications, allowing monitoring and alteration of emails, social media, and phone calls; during post-election protests in June 2009, Iran's Internet access slowed to less than 10% of normal speeds, suspected due to deep packet inspection. In July 2009, Nokia began experiencing a boycott of its products and services in Iran led by consumers supporting the protest movement, resulting in reduced demand for handsets and declining SMS usage. Nokia Siemens Networks stated in a press release that it provided only a "lawful intercept capability solely for monitoring of local voice calls" and denied providing deep packet inspection, web censorship, or Internet filtering. In October 2009, Nokia filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court of Delaware against Apple Inc., claiming infringement of 10 wireless communication patents, including data transfer; Apple responded with a countersuit in December 2009, accusing Nokia of 11 patent infringements.

During the post-election protests in Iran in June 2009, Iran's Internet access slowed to less than a tenth of its normal speeds, which experts suspected was due to the use of deep packet inspection.[279] In July 2009, Nokia began to face a boycott of its products and services in Iran, led by consumers sympathetic to the post-election protest movement and targeting companies perceived as collaborating with the regime; demand for handsets declined and users started avoiding SMS messaging.[280] Nokia Siemens Networks stated in a press release that it provided Iran only with a "lawful intercept capability solely for monitoring of local voice calls" and that it "has not provided any deep packet inspection, web censorship, or Internet filtering capability to Iran".[281] In October 2009, Nokia filed a lawsuit against Apple Inc. in the U.S. District Court of Delaware, claiming that Apple infringed on 10 of its patents related to wireless communication, including data transfer.[282] Apple responded by filing a countersuit in December 2009, accusing Nokia of 11 patent infringements; Apple's general counsel, Bruce Sewell, stated, "Other companies must compete with us by inventing their own technologies, not just by stealing ours." This led to a legal dispute between the two telecom companies, with Nokia later filing another suit with the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC), alleging Apple had infringed its patents in "virtually all of its mobile phones, portable music players and computers," and requesting a ban on all U.S. imports of Apple products, including the iPhone, Macintosh, and iPod.[283] Apple countered by filing a complaint with the ITC in January 2010.[282] In June 2011, Apple settled with Nokia, agreeing to an estimated one-time payment of $600 million and royalties to Nokia, and also reached a cross-licensing agreement on some of their patented technologies.[284][285][286] In January 2013, Nokia's Indian subsidiary was charged with non-payment of Indian Tax Deducted at Source and violating transfer pricing norms in India; the unpaid TDS of ₹30 billion, accumulated over six years, stemmed from royalty payments made by the Indian subsidiary to its parent company.[287][288] In March 2019, it was reported that the Nokia 7 Plus phones were allegedly sending personal user data to China over several months; investigators found that the devices transmitted unencrypted data packages—including geographical location, SIM card number, and phone serial number—to an unidentified Chinese server each time the phone was turned on, the screen activated, or unlocked, enabling real-time tracking of the user's movements and actions.[289] Nokia brand owner HMD Global denied any such data transfers, claiming it was due to an error in the software packing process.[290] The Finnish Office of the Data Protection Ombudsman launched an investigation into the matter, assuming "that personal data has been transferred."[291] In 2020, the Australian Strategic Policy Institute accused at least 82 major brands, including Nokia, of being linked to forced Uyghur labor in Xinjiang.[292]
